The Directors are pleased to present the climate statements of Partners Life Limited (‘PLL’)
for the year ended 31 March 2024.

These climate statements comply with the requirements of the Aotearoa New Zealand
Climate Standards (‘NZ CS’) issued by the External Reporting Board (‘XRB’) and are our
first disclosures under these new Standards.

At this time, climate risk is not a material risk for PLL.

In the short to medium term, Partners Life may experience transition risks indirectly, as
customer finances may be impacted by the transition to a low-carbon economy. In the
medium and long term, physical risks are likely to play a greater role as chronic and acute
weather changes can impact the young and the elderly.

For and on behalf of the Board:

Cautionary note and limitations

This report is a summary of Partners Life's assessment of future climate risks and opportunities. It is naturally forward-looking and is a point-in-
time assessment of the future based on the information available to Partners Life now. We have had to make assumptions that are subject to
inherent risks and uncertainties, many of which are beyond our control and give rise to the possibility that our predictions, expectations or
conclusions will not prove to be accurate, that our assumptions may not be correct, and that our objectives, targets, and strategies to mitigate and
adapt to climate-related risks and opportunities will not be achieved.

We have explained the basis and limitations of our analysis in this report and reserves the right to revisit these assumptions, as we develop our
understanding, without notice. This section should be read together with the limitations identified elsewhere in this Annual Report, including as
described below.

Executive Summary

While we have taken care in preparing these climate statements, we make no representation as to the statement’s accuracy, completeness or
reliability, in particular in relation to Partners Life’s assumptions regarding future events. To the extent possible under New Zealand law, Partners
Life is not liable for any loss (direct, indirect, consequential, or otherwise) or damage arising from the use of this report.

entity must disclose the identity of the governance body 
responsible for oversight of climate-related risks and opportunities, 
a description of their oversight and a description of management’s 
role in assessing and managing climate-related risks and 
opportunities1.
Governance body
PLL’s  corporate governance structure is set out in Figure 1. The 
Board delegates its responsibilities relating to risk management to 
the Board Risk Committee (‘BRC’). The BRC is responsible for 
overseeing the climate-related risks and opportunities. 
Governance body oversight 
In early 2023, PLL engaged a provider to run a series of 
educational workshops with the BRC to improve skills and 
competency and to ensure the BRC has an understanding of 
climate change impacts. 
The BRC considers sustainability as a regular agenda item on its 
work plan. In addition, the BRC is informed about climate-related 
risks and opportunities through a dedicated sustainability report 
presented by management semi-annually This includes climate 
risk information to assist the BRC in its oversight of climate-related 
risks and opportunities.
The role of management
Management is accountable for the sub-risk registers and for the 
treatment and continued management of risks within each 
business unit.
The 
Management 
Risk 
Committee 
(‘MRC’) 
supports 
the 
management, monitoring and oversight of risk management 
activities within the business. The MRC meets bi-monthly with 
standing agenda items including reviewing identified and emerging 
risks and the control environment. Climate risk matters are 
considered and form part of the discussion during MRC meetings, 
consistent with other material risks. Management provides updates 
on risks to the BRC, which meets four times a year (at minimum).

text:
To achieve compliance with the Strategy disclosure requirements 
of NZ CS 1, an entity must disclose a description of the climate-
related risks and opportunities it has identified over the short, 
medium and long term as well as current impacts.  Scenario 
analysis must be undertaken to inform this assessment and a 
transition plan on how it will position itself as the global and 
domestic economy transitions towards a low-emissions, climate-
resilient future state must be disclosed2. 
PLL’s business model & strategy
PLL’s business model is centred on offering a diverse range of 
insurance products designed to financially protect individuals and  
businesses in New Zealand from various life and health-related 
risks.
Our products include life and terminal illness covers, trauma 
covers (including trauma, moderate, and severe), disability covers 
(including income cover - indemnity and agreed value, mortgage 
repayment cover, income and expenses cover), total and 
permanent disability cover, specific condition cover, private medical 
cover, and group schemes (such as employer provided covers for 
employees and bespoke benefit cover for defined members), 
designed to provide a lump sum in the event of death, or either a 
lump sum or monthly payment to clients who are diagnosed with  
serious health events, unable to work due to illness or injury either 
for a period of a time or permanently, or to fast-track access to 
medical treatment privately.
Current physical and transition impacts of climate 
change
Recent extreme weather events have impacted the general 
insurance sector3 and the broader economy. The impact on life and 
health insurance providers is harder to assess. Increasing extreme 
weather events could lead to increased health risks, which, in turn, 
could lead to increased demand for cover and increase insurance 
claims. They could also cause disruptions to distribution channels 
reducing the overall volume of insurance purchased. The potential 
impacts of these risks are difficult to quantify.
Scenario analysis 
1.Sector-level collaboration
PLL joined the Financial Services Council (‘FSC’) initiative to 
develop scenario narratives for the financial services sector and 
was actively involved with their development.
2.Focal question
PLL formulated a focal question (as recommended in the Financial 
Markets Authority (‘FMA’) guidance) to guide the analysis, aligning 
with strategic objectives and risk management priorities: How 
could climate change affect our business model, impact on our 
mid-term strategy, and what actions may be necessary to address 
these impacts?
3.Scenarios chosen
PLL used scenarios from the sector scenario narratives: 1.5°C 
‘Orderly’, 2°C 'Too Little Too Late', and 3°C 'Hothouse' due to our 
familiarity with the scenarios (having been involved in their 
development), widespread global usage, comparability within the 
New Zealand financial services sector, and the availability of data. 
We used this data, along with the rationale and emission 
pathways4 for each scenario as described at the FSC sector level.
4.Downscaling sector scenario analysis
We ran an introductory workshop with senior executives on 
scenario analysis. Following this, a management working group  
analysed the sector scenarios, focusing on their specific 
parameters. This involved identifying relevant climate drivers  and 
their impact on PLL.
5.Scenario analysis workshops
We conducted a series of workshops to identify climate-related 
risks and opportunities arising from the selected scenarios. The 
key steps in the workshops included (1) analysing the three 
climate-related scenarios downscaled for PLL, (2) reviewing 
identified material risks and their materiality, (3) assessing climate 
risks against PLL’s mid-term strategy, and (4) evaluating the risk 
impacts and discussing opportunities across three time horizons 
and three climate-related scenarios.
Our risk assessment took into account their potential impacts of 
the scenarios on strategic objectives, business operation, and the 
established risk tolerance of PLL. The scenario analysis workshop 
process and key findings were presented to the BRC, together with 
monitoring of how climate risks are continuing to transform over 
time.

Climate-change scenarios
Orderly

Under the ‘Orderly’ 1.5°C scenario, a worldwide 
collective effort is underway to reduce emissions. 
These efforts will involve the introduction of new 
legislation that bans high emitters like petrol/diesel 
vehicles, shifts in consumer preferences, and 
increased emission prices. Under this scenario, the 
physical risks associated with climate change will be 
limited due to the global collective effort. However, 
transition risks will be intensified in the short and 
medium term as the economy shifts towards a low-
carbon model.
As New Zealand transitions to a low-carbon economy 
the broader economic effects will be significant. For 
instance, a rise in carbon taxes on sectors like energy 
and agriculture will lead to higher oil prices, affecting 
transportation and the overall economy. Additionally, 
food prices are expected to surge in the short and 
medium term leading to increased inflation. This, in 
turn, will affect customers’ ability to afford essentials 
like life and health insurance, thereby influencing the 
sales of new policies. This scenario also offers 
benefits such as reduced medical claims resulting 
from  healthier lifestyles and decreased air pollution.
Under the ‘Too Little Too Late’ (2°C) scenario, some 
countries, including New Zealand, take proactive 
measures to address climate change, while others 
lag behind before eventually taking more aggressive 
action. As extreme weather becomes more severe, 
there is aggressive global action in the medium- and 
long  term to reduce emissions.
In this scenario, the rate of physical risks due to 
climate change increases steadily over time, while 
transition risks spike early, stabilise as net-zero 
targets are met domestically, and then rise again due 
to global action and new decarbonisation 
technologies. 
Mental health impacts, including climate anxiety, will 
rise due to increasing extreme weather events. These 
physical and transition risks will increase morbidity in 
the medium to long term, affecting life and health 
insurance claims and costs. In the long term 
independent financial advisers may face challenges 
with access to customers due to extreme weather 
events, potentially altering distribution channels.
Finally, reinsurers in progressive countries will face 
increased risks, making reinsurance more costly and 
difficult for New Zealand insurers, especially those 
not aligned with net-zero targets.
Under the ‘Hothouse’ 3°C scenario, there is minimal 
action towards a low carbon global transition. Despite 
increasing levels of social, economic, and 
environmental degradation, there is little shift in social 
and political traction towards a low emissions future. 
In this scenario, extreme weather events become 
more frequent and intense. As communities suffer 
from frequent extreme weather events impacting their 
lives, they will be preoccupied with the aftermath, 
which will adversely affect new policy sales for life 
and health insurers. 
Increased exposure to heat stress in certain regions 
will lead to a higher occurrence of cardiovascular and 
respiratory diseases, along with a rise in skin cancer 
cases. Additionally, the changing climate, becoming 
warmer and wetter in some places, will increase the 
ability of vector-borne diseases to spread, thereby 
escalating the frequency and cases of severe 
infectious diseases. This will lead to overwhelmed 
public health systems, resulting in longer queues and 
extended waiting times for medical care. 
Consequently, customers are likely to place a higher 
value on health and life insurance policies, leading to 
an increase in policy sales.

Scenario analysis assumptions & limitations
The FSC sector-level analysis made certain assumptions and had 
certain limitations. Two of these limitations in particular are 
applicable to PLL:
—There is a discrepancy between global and domestic climate 
outcomes even when similar scenario narratives are used. A 
fundamental challenge is the differences in modelling 
approaches at the global and domestic levels for calculating 
scenario parameters. Moreover, the projections for New 
Zealand’s response to climate change differ from those for the 
rest of the world. Such discrepancies are largely inevitable 
when integrating multiple independent scenarios.
—The pace at which climate-related impacts are unfolding is 
unparalleled, making historical data less reliable for evaluating 
their extent and patterns. Consequently, this introduces a 
greater degree of uncertainty for insurers in determining the 
scale and timing of climate risk factors. Moreover, these factors 
are prone to tipping points that further amplify uncertainty, 
especially considering the geographical variation in physical 
and transition impacts both in New Zealand and globally.

opportunities
Our climate-related risks, opportunities, and impacts over time 
are outlined in the tables below. PLL’s impact assessment matrix 
was used to determine the risk ratings. After existing risk

residual.
For the life and health insurance business, the physical impacts 
of climate change are more significant than transition risks. 
Physical risks are expected to worsen over the medium and long 
term under a scenario where global temperatures rise by 3°C.

Transition plan

To achieve compliance with the Risk Management disclosure 
requirements of NZ CS 1, an entity must disclose a description of 
its processes for identifying, assessing, and managing climate-
related risks and how these processes are integrated into its 
overall risk management processes5.
PLL’s Risk Management Programme (‘RMP’) outlines our risk 
identification, assessment, and management processes. Climate-
risk is managed through this process.
Figure 2: Risk Management Framework Components
Risk identification
PLL considers risks across its entire value chain.
Risk identification can occur at any point during day-to-day 
activities in the business and is the responsibility of all employees. 
This is supplemented by scheduled annual risk workshops guided 
by the Risk and Compliance team. The Risk and Compliance team 
also conducts an external risk scan on a regular basis to monitor 
emerging external risks.
Risks are separated into seven categories and risk appetite 
statements exist for each of these:
—Strategic
—Insurance/Product
—Financial
—Operational
—Conduct
—Regulatory
—Compliance/Legal 
Risk assessment 
PLL considers risks across its entire value chain.
Risks are evaluated from two perspectives: likelihood of 
occurrence and impact. This likelihood of occurrence is assessed 
by considering the probability of the risk occurring and the impact 
is assessed by using a consistent rating scale incorporating both 
quantitative and qualitative measures. We consider both the 
inherent and residual ratings in determining the overall risk 
associated with a given event.
Risk management
Risks are monitored by risk owners on a regular basis through 
measurement of key risk indicators (‘KRI’). this applies to all key 
risks for PLL. At this stage, there are no KRIs for climate risk 
because climate risk is not currently a key risk for PLL. 
KRI owners provide the data to support monitoring and they (or the 
risk owners) supply commentary to support and explain such 
movements. Where risk exposure is outside risk appetite, a risk 
treatment plan is required to be put in place. There is oversight 
over KRI and risk treatment plan reporting in the MRC and BRC.
Our process for identifying and assessing climate-related 
risks
PLL employs a comprehensive approach for climate risk 
assessment, integrating internal evaluations through scenario 
analysis, third-party research, and industry insights. The scenario 
analysis previously described is our primary tool for identifying 
climate-related risks. We treat climate risk as a sub-category of 
strategic risk with its own corresponding risk appetite statement. 
The scenario analysis process and risk appetite statements are to 
be repeated and reviewed, respectively, on a yearly basis going 
forward
Frequency of management engagement on climate issues
— Climate risk matters are considered and form part of the 
discussion during MRC meetings (bi-monthly), where relevant, 
consistent with other material risks.
— Annual risk workshops help to identify and prioritise climate-
related risks.
Prioritising climate-related risks 
We prioritise activity to manage risk based on the inherent and 
residual ratings of the risk and with reference to our Board-set risk 
appetite.

PLL does not have exposure to high-emission sectors such as 
fossil fuels and materials, as all our investments are in cash and 
sovereign bonds.
 Targets
For the first year of reporting, we have decided not to establish 
emission targets due to the following reasons:
Investment emission target
The financed emissions from our investments are minimal, given 
our lack of exposure to high-emission asset classes or sectors. 
PLL is committed to conducting an annual analysis of our portfolio 
and will consider setting targets in the future if deemed necessary.
Operational emission target
In our first year of reporting PLL has applied the NZ CS 3 adoptive 
provision to our Scope 3 emissions, except for business travel and 
investment emissions.
PLL was acquired by Dai-ichi Life International Holdings LLC 
(‘DIL’) in 2022. As we continue to evaluate the applicable Scope 3 
emission categories specific to our operations and our integration 
into the DIL group progresses, we have opted to not set any 
operational emission targets at this time. In future years, we will be 
in a better position next year to establish meaningful and informed 
targets.
11
source: Partners Life Limited Climate Statements 31 March 2024 (stand alone).pdf

text:
Assessment Report 6 (AR6): The sixth assessment report by the 
IPCC, summarising the latest scientific findings on climate change.
Climate Change Commission (‘CCC’): The CCC is an 
independent Crown entity that advises the New Zealand 
Government on climate change policy and monitors the 
government's progress towards New Zealand's emission reduction 
goals within the framework of the Climate Change Response 
Amendment Act.
Data Quality Score: Within the PCAF standards, data quality is 
categorised on a scale from 1 to 5. ‘Data Quality 1’ represents the 
highest level of data quality, while ‘Data Quality 5’ indicates the 
lowest.
Financed emission: Absolute emissions that banks and investors 
finance through their loans and investments.
GHG Protocol: A widely used international accounting tool to 
understand, quantify, and manage greenhouse gas emissions.
Global Warming Potentials (‘GWP’): A measure that compares 
the impact of emitting one ton of a greenhouse gas to one ton of 
carbon dioxide over a specified period, used to understand and 
compare the impact of different gases on global warming.
Greenhouse Gas (‘GHG’) Emissions: Emissions of gases that 
trap heat in the atmosphere, causing the greenhouse effect. Major 
GHGs include carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), and nitrous 
oxide (N2O).
International Energy Agency (‘IEA’): The IEA is a Paris-based 
autonomous intergovernmental organisation that provides policy 
recommendations, analysis and data on the global energy sector
Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (‘IPCC’): The 
United Nations body responsible for assessing the science related 
to climate change, providing a scientific basis for governments to 
develop climate-related policies.
IPCC SSP1-1.9: This is IPCC’s sustainability scenario; this 
describes a world where global CO2 emissions are cut to net zero 
around 2050.
IPCC SSP2-4.5: This is IPCC’s ‘middle of the road’ IPCC scenario. 
Under this scenario, CO2 emissions hover around current levels 
before starting to fall mid-century, but do not reach net-zero by 
2100.
IPCC SSP5-8.5: This is IPCC’s ‘fossil fueled development’ 
scenario, Under this scenario, CO2 emission triple by 2075 from 
current level.
Land Use, Land-Use Change, and Forestry (‘LULUCF’): is 
defined as a greenhouse gas inventory sector that covers 
emissions and removals of greenhouse gases resulting from direct 
human-induced land use such as settlements and commercial 
uses, land-use change, and forestry activities. 
Nationally Determined Target Contribution (‘NDC’): Individual 
country commitments to reduce national emissions and adapt to 
the impacts of climate change, as part of the Paris Agreement.
The National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research 
(‘NIWA’): NIWA is a New Zealand Crown Research Institute 
focusing on environmental science related to water, atmosphere, 
and climate, supporting sustainable resource management.
Network for Greening the Financial System(‘NGFS’): NGFS is a 
network of central banks and financial supervisors aimed at 
enhancing the role of the financial system in managing risks and 
mobilizing capital for green and low-carbon investments in the 
context of environmentally sustainable development.
Paris Agreement: The Paris Agreement, adopted within the 
UNFCCC in December 2015, commits participating countries to 
limit global temperature rise to well-below 2°C above pre-industrial 
levels and pursue efforts to limit warming to 1.5°C, adapt to 
changes already occurring, and regularly increase efforts over 
time. 
Partnership for Carbon Accounting Financials (‘PCAF’): An 
initiative to standardise carbon accounting for the financial sector, 
enabling financial institutions to assess and disclose greenhouse 
gas emissions associated with their loans and investments.
Representative 
Concentration 
Pathways 
(‘RCP’): 
The 
Representative Concentration Pathways were developed around 
2010 by the global climate science community. They provide a 
common set of ‘concentration pathways’: descriptions of the 
amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, both historically and 
into the future by year - from 2005 throught to 2300.
Scope 1 Emission: Direct GHG emissions that occur from 
sources owned or controlled by the reporting company, i.e., 
emissions from combustion in owned or controlled boilers, 
furnaces, vehicles, etc.
Scope 2 Emission: Indirect GHG emissions from the generation 
of purchased or acquired electricity, steam, heating, or cooling 
consumed by the reporting company. Scope 2 emissions physically 
occur at the facility where the electricity, steam, heating, or cooling 
is generated.
Scope 3 category 15 (investments) emissions: This category 
includes scope 3 emissions associated with the reporting 
company’s loans and investments in the reporting year, not already 
included in scope 1 or scope 2.
Scope 3 Emission: All other indirect GHG emissions (not included 
in Scope 2) that occur in the value chain of the reporting company. 
Scope 3 can be broken down into upstream emissions and 
downstream emissions.
Shared socioeconomic pathways (‘SSP’): The SSPs are a set of 
five scenarios which were developed by the global climate science 
community around 2015. SSPs include a wide range of 
socioeconomic factors, like population and GDP.
tCO2e: tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent
UNFCCC: The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate 
Change.
